question_type: OLS linear projection (four Jan-31 schedule points, 1948-1951, projected to 1952) of the fixed-maturity amount in the public marketable securities maturity schedule

opus_divergence.what_opus_did: Opus read 'values of ... securities ... that are of fixed maturity type ... as of the maturity schedule' as the whole outstanding fixed-maturity amount. For each Jan 31 schedule (Debt Operations Table 1, March 1948-1951 issues) it summed the 'Total' rows of the 'Fixed maturity issues' column across every maturity year, plus one fixed bond listed without a year total. It cross-checked each sum against the by-type debt table in the same issue, then fit OLS on 1948-1951 and projected 1952. It explicitly considered the 'current-year maturities only' reading and rejected it.
opus_divergence.what_right_glm_did: The cards arm used the same March-issue Jan 31 schedules but took only the first 'Total' row of the 'Fixed maturity issues' column. That row covers the fixed-maturity issues maturing in the schedule's own calendar year, one printed cell per schedule. It fit OLS on those four values.
opus_divergence.evidence: Opus calc.py:14-42 (per-year totals summed per schedule), calc.py:76-80 (current-year-only reading computed only as an '[alt]'); transcripts/solver.jsonl StructuredOutput key_decisions item 2 ('the total of all fixed-maturity issues across every maturity year, not just the ones maturing in the current year'); review.md:24 (current-year reading 'rejected'); cards [89] (OLS on the four first-row totals), [90] (rationale: 'those are the values visible in the table for each year')

reviewer_flag: Verdict 'confirmed'. The reviewer re-derived the same sums with an independent by-type cross-check and named only pre-rounding of inputs as a residual risk. It considered the current-year-only reading and rejected it because 'the question asks for the fixed-maturity amount, not just near-term maturities' (review.md:24). Nothing was flagged about the actual failure mode.
right_by_principled_choice_or_luck: Partly luck. Cards first tried the full-sum reading but double-counted callable issues; it noticed that its sum was larger than total marketable debt ([76], [84]) and never produced a correct full sum. It then fell back to the first-row totals with a salience argument at [90] and a shaky rationale at [92]. It landed on the single printed cell per schedule, which is how the reference was built, but it never weighed that against a correct version of the reading Opus used. No card in its deck covers maturity schedules.
wrong_glm_arms_same_as_opus: prompt: yes on interpretation. Like Opus, it summed the per-year fixed-maturity totals across maturity years ([32]-[45], [53]-[59]). It left out a right-half year total in the 1950 schedule ([39]-[41], [63]), so its projection is different from Opus's and also wrong. none: no. It leaned toward the same current-year reading as cards ([70]), but it read the January issues instead of the March issues that carry the Jan 31 schedules ([11], [14]). The January issues' schedules are 'Outstanding November 30' of the previous year (e.g. treasury_bulletin_1949_01.txt:1371). OCR-misaligned cells made it worse ([35]-[44], [58]). Its error is SOURCE_ISSUE_VINTAGE plus extraction.
lesson_for_harness: For 'value as of a maturity schedule' questions, the reference used the 'Total' row for the schedule's own calendar year: one printed cell per schedule, not an aggregate across maturity years that the solver builds. Question UID0117 (ordinal 9) was built the same way, and its wording said so explicitly ('scheduled to mature in that calendar year'). The prompt arm had that precedent in context as L-pdo1-maturity-total-rows but did not transfer it here. General lesson: when a question names a series 'as of' a table and does not ask for a total over the table, prefer a single printed cell whose label matches over a sum the solver constructs. If the answer needs an aggregate the table never prints, that should trigger an interpretation CHECK ('is this a printed cell or a constructed aggregate?') and a STATE lookup of the conventions already learned for this table family.
notes: The two readings give projections about 45% apart, so the grader cleanly separates them. Opus's reading is semantically defensible, but the question is not on the disputed list, so the single-cell construction should be treated as the benchmark's convention for this table family. The cards final answer carried a unit suffix and was still graded correct. The Opus evidence for this ordinal comes only from calc.py, review.md and the solver transcript, because the worklog and solution files were never written.
